s.d: the illegitimate offspring of unmarried parents
A blow struck to the side or from the side, as in swordplay; a secondary or incidental strike of any sort.
x: Either commander took speedy advantage of it—Hopton to make a swift diversion into Sussex and capture Arundel Castle (which was but a by-blow, for in a few weeks he had lost it again).
As a by-blow in the course of his relentless campaigns against Louis, Willem gained the three thrones of Britain in 1699 – but what a by-blow this proved!

s.d: (slang) An illegitimate child; a child of an unknown or unmarried father.
x: The best hope has been that friends and family would talk, a hope partly realized in this discreet but perceptive memoir by his illegitimate daughter. . . . Little Mary was a by-blow and an inconvenience.

x: Coordinate term: general election
In 2015, he was selected as candidate for that year's by-election for the Oldham West and Royton seat. He won with 62% of the vote.

x: he had a bye in the first round

s.d: a farewell remark
x: they said their good-byes

s.d: The position of a person or team in a tournament or competition who draws no opponent in a particular round so advances to the next round unopposed, or is awarded points for a win in a league table; also the phantom opponent of such a person or team.
x: Craig's Crew plays the bye next week.
The Patriots were in the unique situation of having to play 16 straight games, then have their bye in week 17, whether they needed it or not.

s.d: An extra scored when the batsmen take runs after the ball has passed the striker without hitting either the bat or the batsman.
(obsolete) A thing not directly aimed at; a secondary or subsidiary object, course, path, undertaking, issue, etc.
x: The Synod of Dort in some points condemneth, upon the by, even the discipline of the Church of England.

s.d: (Scotland) An unspecified way or place.
x: Frank Kennedy will shew you the penalties in the act, and ye ken yoursell they used to put their run goods into the auld Place of Ellangowan up bye there.
This was lattin at me, ye ken, for inveetin the coachman an' the gamekeeper up bye.

s.d: A pass.
A command to exit a session.
Out of the way; remote.
x: At length having gained a very bye Alley, where he thought he might enter into a Conference unnoticed by any who knew him.

s.d: Secondary; supplementary.
x: It is the custom in some provinces to pay only according to the basic crops produced, but in others the share is calculated out of the total produce of the farm, both bye and main products.

s.d: (colloquial) Goodbye.
(slang) An exclamation of disbelief or dismissal.
x: “Okay, busted. But you see all them muscles, girl?” She shakes her head, laughing. “Nope. I only have eyes for my boo.” “Girl, bye. You can still look.” She giggles. “Well, I ain’t lookin’ hard, trust.[…]”
Rowlings-Blake responded: "Girl bye, if he can't take criticism from 'a joke', what's he gonna do when somebody real comes for him? #notready"

From by (adverb) + gone. See go by.

s.d: past events to be put aside
x: let bygones be bygones

s.d: An event that happened in the past.
x: Jennie Fox watched it with thoughtful pleasure, and the rest were chatting and telling of bygones, enjoying a glass of egg-hot; it being a custom for them to partake of this beverage on this particular night.

s.d: An object from the past; a relic, antique, etc.
x: And now just as the Victorians collected the minute objects with which to fill these houses, so today grown-ups are paying large sums for these bygones, while the children are given more modern houses to play with.

s.d: well in the past; former
x: bygone days
dreams of foregone times

s.d: Having been or happened in the distant past.
x: Near by he could see the thicket of raspberry canes, growing tall and close like a tropical jungle, in whose shadow he had played with the Boy on bygone mornings.

bylaw.e: From Middle English bylawe, bilawe, partly from Old English bīlage (“bylaw”) and partly from a variant of Middle English byrelawe, birlawe, from Old Norse býjar (“town's; settlement's”) + lǫg (“laws; jurisdiction”). Byrlaw is attested earlier in English but is unattested in Old Norse and the cognates in Scandinavian languages follow the development of bylaw: Danish bylov (“municipal law”), Swedish bylag and byalag.

s.d: a rule adopted by an organization in order to regulate its own affairs and the behavior of its members
A local custom or law of a settlement or district.
A rule made by a local authority to regulate its own affairs.
A law or rule governing the internal affairs of an organization (e.g., corporation or business).

byname.e: From by- + name. Cognate with Dutch bijnaam (“nickname”), German Beiname (“nickname, epithet”), Swedish binamn, Danish binavn and Norwegian Bokmål binavn.

s.d: a familiar name for a person (often a shortened version of a person's given name)
x: Joe's mother would not use his nickname and always called him Joseph
Henry's nickname was Slim

s.d: Any secondary name, particularly: Synonym of epithet, a descriptive and distinguishing additional name.
x: Lions-heart, is... the by-name of K. Richard.

s.d: Any secondary name, particularly: A formal epithet for a god or goddess, used in rituals in Heathenry.
(Scotland, UK, dialectal) Any secondary name, particularly: Synonym of pseudonym, a second name used to disguise authorship etc.
(archaic) Any secondary name, particularly: Synonym of nickname, an informal personal name.
(archaic, historical) Any secondary name, particularly: Synonym of cognomen, a personal or hereditary additional name in ancient Roman contexts.
x: Eutropius... gives him the additional name of Crinitus, perhaps a by-name of his family.

s.d: (archaic) To assign a byname to.

bypass.e: From Middle English *bypassen, *bipassen (suggested by past participle by-past, bipast), equivalent to by- + pass.

s.d: a highway that encircles an urban area so that traffic does not have to pass through the center
a surgically created shunt (usually around a damaged part)
a conductor having low resistance in parallel with another device to divert a fraction of the current
A road that passes around something, such as a residential area or business district.
A replacement road for obsolete road that is no longer in use because devastating natural disasters (earthquakes, tsunamis, landslides).
The act of going past or around.
A section of pipe that conducts a fluid around some other fixture.
An electrical shunt.
An alternative passage created to divert a bodily fluid around a damaged organ; the surgical procedure to construct such a bypass.
x: Five of the 16 patients required simultaneous FF bypass and iliaco-femoral bypass; 2, required simultaneous FF bypass and iliac thrombo-endoarterectomy (Table II).

s.d: avoid something unpleasant or laborious
x: You cannot bypass these rules!

s.d: To avoid an obstacle etc, by constructing or using a bypass.
To ignore the usual channels or procedures.
x: More to theyr proper Elements inaugurated none, / Than ſhee to hers by-paſſed, he to his poſſeſſed Throne.
Datacasting bypasses the wired, terrestrial Internet and is a cheaper way to distribute software than pressing and mailing CDs.

a capacitor that provides low impedance over certain (high) frequencies
well in the past; former
x: bygone days
dreams of foregone times

s.d: past
x: The Hospital […] for these two bypast years has contained not less than 150 beds, generally occupied by a full amount of patients.

bypath.e: Inherited from Middle English bypath; by surface analysis, by + path.

s.d: a side road little traveled (as in the countryside)
An unfrequented path; an indirect route; a byway.
x: Having gone to Chiang Chou from Chü-wo by the northern route through Hou-ma, we returned over a bypath through mountains in the south which has been gradually elevated from the Fêng River valley by loess deposit.

During these days, the boy rode Sir Mortimer abroad in many directions until he knew every bypath within a radius of fifty miles of Torn. Sometimes the old man accompanied him, but more often he rode alone.

s.d: incidental activity performed by an actor for dramatic effect
x: his business with the cane was hilarious

s.d: (uncountable) Any action, carried out onstage during a performance, apart from the main action.
x: [...] there had been some amusing byplay with the enginemen as to what might be expected to happen if the engines failed to behave themselves properly.
The father-son byplay is occasionally overdone and tedious, but there is a genuine warmth in both the Oland-Luke and the Toler-Sen Yung teamings.

s.d: (uncountable) Any action, by supporting actor.
a secondary and sometimes unexpected consequence
a product made during the manufacture of something else

byre.e: From Middle English bire, bier, byr, from Old English bȳre.

s.d: a barn for cows
(UK) A barn, especially one used for keeping cattle in.
x:
It was here in the kitchen, in the passage,
In the mews in the harn in the byre in the market-place [...]
The visitors came up the narrow road through the forest from the south; they filled the spare-rooms, they bunked out in cow byres and barns.

byrnie.e: From Middle English brinie, burne (whence also, without metathesis, obsolete English brinie), from Old Norse brynja. Cognates include Old English byrne, Gothic 𐌱𐍂𐌿𐌽𐌾𐍉 (brunjō) (whence Old Church Slavonic брънѩ (brŭnję)), German Brünne, French broigne.

s.d: a long (usually sleeveless) tunic of chain mail formerly worn as defensive armor
(historical) A short chain mail shirt, covering from the upper arms to the upper thighs.
x: […] those that walked armed before the Witches’ booths, six in company, harnessed as for battle in byrnies of shining bronze, with greaves and shields of bronze and helms that glanced in the sun.
It was the Viking habit. Even as a man plowed his field or chopped trees in the woods, his byrnie and his sword were always at hand.

A road less frequented than a highway; a byway.

s.d: tuft of strong filaments by which e.g. a mussel makes itself fast to a fixed surface
(uncountable) The long fine silky filaments excreted by several mollusks (particularly Pinna nobilis) by which they attach themselves to the sea bed, and from which sea silk is manufactured.
(uncountable) Sea silk manufactured from these filaments.
(uncountable) The stipe or stem of some fungi which are particularly thin and thread-like.
a nonparticipant spectator
A person who, although present at some event, does not take part in it; an observer, witness, or spectator.
x: Conservative influencer Nick Sortor is handcuffed Thursday night by a police officer outside an ICE facility in Portland, Oregon, a bystander video shows; the video does not show events leading up to the arrest.

byte.e: An alteration of the word bite so it would not be accidentally misspelled as bit. Coined by Werner Buchholz in 1956, during the early design phase for the IBM 7030 Stretch computer.

s.d: a sequence of 8 bits (enough to represent one character of alphanumeric data) processed as a single unit of information
A short sequence of bits (binary digits) that can be operated on as a unit by a computer; the smallest usable machine word.
A unit of computing storage equal to eight bits, which can represent any of 256 distinct values.
x: The word “hello” fits into five bytes of ASCII code.

byway.e: From Middle English bywey, equivalent to by- + way.

s.d: a side road little traveled (as in the countryside)
A road or track not following a main route; a secondary or minor road or path.
x: Near-synonyms: back road, back street, back lane
Although some of its individuality has been lost, this railway byway in North Essex still retains its charm, and is well worthy of exploration by railway enthusiasts.

s.d: A road that is not frequently travelled.
a little-known or arcane field of study or detail.
x: Though his account of written communication over the past 5,000 years necessarily has a powerful forward momentum, his diversions down the fascinating byways of the subject are irresistible ...

byword.e: From Middle English byword, byworde (“proverb”), from Old English bīword, bīwyrd, bīwyrde (“proverb, household word", also "adverb”), from Proto-West Germanic *bīwurdī, equivalent to by- + word. Compare Latin proverbium, which byword may possibly be a translation of. Cognate with Old High German pīwurti (“proverb”). Compare also Old English bīspel (“proverb, example”), bīcwide (“byword, proverb, tale, fable”), Dutch bijwoord (“adverb”).

s.d: a condensed but memorable saying embodying some important fact of experience that is taken as true by many people
A proverb or proverbial expression, common saying; a frequently used word or phrase.
A characteristic word or expression; a word or phrase associated with a person or group.
Someone or something that stands as an example (i.e. metonymically) for something else, by having some of that something's characteristic traits.
x: Illustrious unfortunates attract a wider sympathy, not because their griefs are more intense, but because, being set on lofty pedestals, they the better serve mankind as instances and bywords of calamity.

s.d: An object of notoriety or contempt, scorn or derision.
x: He hath made me also a byword of the people […]
"I know you and Harry are inseparable. Surely for that reason, if for none other, you should not have made his sister's name a by-word."

s.d: A nickname or epithet.
a gold coin of the Byzantine Empire; widely circulated in Europe in the Middle Ages
